In-line PCBA cleaning · after wave soldering, reflow and hand solder

Flux residues in. Clean boards out.
One pass. Nine sections. No scrubbing bench.

The SME-6300 is a fully automatic in-line spray cleaning machine for PCBA. Boards ride a stainless steel net conveyor through pre-wash, high-pressure wash, chemical isolation, three DI-water rinse stages, air blow and two hot-air dry sections — and leave the machine ready for conformal coating, testing or assembly. One operator loads the line; the chemistry does the rest.

01 — Why it matters

The residue you cannot see is the failure you will pay for

After wave soldering or reflow, a board can look perfectly clean and still carry rosin films, no-clean flux residues, solder balls and hand-solder flux. Those residues drive corrosion, electromigration, poor probe contact in ICT and coating delamination after conformal coating. Cleaning is not cosmetic — it is a reliability step, and doing it in-line keeps it repeatable.

01

Residues cause failures weeks later

Rosin and no-clean flux residues are hygroscopic. Under humidity and bias they support electrochemical migration — dendrites that short pads apart long after the board left your line. The field failure costs the board, the assembly, the warranty claim and the customer.

02

Manual scrubbing is not a process

A bench brush and solvent removes what the operator had time to reach. There is no logged temperature, no controlled pressure, no repeatable rinse. Two shifts produce two different cleanliness levels on the same product — and ion contamination is invisible until it fails.

03

Batch cleaning breaks the flow

Offline basket machines stop boards between processes and add handling. An in-line cleaner sits on the conveyor itself: boards flow from solder to clean without queues, without re-staging and without a second touch that damages components.

02 — The process

Nine sections, one pass, zero re-handling

Boards enter on the SUS304 net conveyor and travel through nine functional sections in a single pass. Chemistry is applied where it works best — immersion and high-pressure spray for flux removal, staged DI-water rinses to recover ions and chemicals, air knives to stop carryover, and hot air to leave the board dry. Section lengths below are quoted from the 2021 manual.

01

Pre-wash · 380 mm

Water-based cleaning liquid is sprayed top and bottom through 2 + 2 SUS304 spray bars to immerse and soften flux and dust, lowering the work the main wash has to do. The pre-wash shares the 240 L wash tank and recirculates through a steel filter net plus a 1 µm filter barrel.

02

Wash · 560 mm

The main wash: 6 upper and 6 lower spray bars with 72 nozzles form a liquid curtain at 2–8 bar, peeled off by a 5.5 kW SUS304 pump. The 36 kW heater brings the liquid to up to 80 °C, which is what actually dissolves rosin and no-clean residue films.

03

Chemical isolation · 360 mm

Three SUS304 air knives on a 10 HP blower blow wash liquid off the board and back into the wash tank. This is the section that keeps chemistry out of the rinse stages — it protects rinse water quality and pulls the liquid carryover cost back down.

04

Pre-rinse · 400 mm

DI water in a 60 L tank, sprayed through 3 + 3 bars (36 nozzles) at 2–5 bar, takes the remaining liquid film off the board and keeps it out of the rinse stages. Pre-rinse water is continuously refreshed by overflow from the rinse tank.

05

Rinse · 240 mm

The main rinse: a 40 L heated DI-water tank (12 kW, up to 60 °C) and upper/lower spray bars wash ions and particles off the pad geometry. Rinse water recirculates through a steel filter net and is refreshed from the final-rinse overflow.

06

Final rinse · 240 mm

Fresh incoming DI water (≥ 10 MΩ·cm) sprays the board one last time at 1–3 bar. An inline resistivity meter (0–18 MΩ·cm) and a flow meter watch the incoming water quality and consumption in real time — if DI water goes bad, the machine alarms instead of shipping dirty boards.

07

Air blow dry · 600 mm

Two 7.5 HP blowers drive upper and lower air knives that sheet the standing water off the board and back to the rinse tanks, so the hot-air stages only have to remove a thin film. Less heat, less energy, faster cycles.

08

Hot air dry 1 · 570 mm

A 1.2 HP blower circulates air through two 7.5 kW SUS316 heaters; six upper and six lower air knives direct hot air (up to 100 °C) across both board faces. Recirculated hot air dries the board without baking fresh energy into the exhaust.

09

Hot air dry 2 · 570 mm

The second identical hot-air stage gives the through-holes, connector bodies and heatsink shadows time to release trapped water. Boards leave the machine dry to the touch and ready for coating, test or packing.

Section lengths, tank capacities, nozzle counts and temperatures are quoted from the SME-6300 manual (2021), chapter 3.

Why the build is stainless

SUS304 frame, argon-arc welded

No PP or PVC structure parts. The frame resists hot alkaline chemistry, hot water and the mechanical load of a full production line without warping or ageing.

SUS316 heaters

Immersion-type SUS316 heaters in the wash and rinse tanks bring liquid to temperature quickly with ±3 °C PID control, so chemistry works at the temperature that was validated.

Mismatched nozzle rows

Nozzles sit vertically on each bar and are offset between neighbouring bars, so the spray curtain covers component shadows instead of leaving dry patches behind tall parts.

Quick-clamp spray bars

Every spray bar lifts out without tools for cleaning or nozzle changes — maintenance time shows up as production hours, not weekend work.

Tilted tank floors

Water tanks are tilted to the drain so they empty fully at changeover. No standing water sitting in a corner between runs.

Observation glass everywhere

Inner and outer doors carry windows so operators watch the spray, rinse and dry stages live; good seals keep water and vapour inside the machine.

The control system protects the board and the operator

Recipes, not guesswork

Conveyor speed, spray pressures, liquid and rinse temperatures and hot-air temperature are set on the touch panel and can be saved per product.

Alarms with addresses

Three-colour stack, buzzer and on-screen fault text. Board-drop detection at input and output, low-water heater protection and DI resistivity alarms all name the cause.

Soft starts and UPS run-out

Electric devices start two seconds apart to cut inrush current; a UPS keeps the conveyor running so loaded boards exit safely if power drops.

MES-ready (option)

An optional MES interface lets the line log cleaning as a real process step — recipe used, temperatures held, alarms raised.

04 — Capacity

The throughput maths, honestly

An in-line cleaner is paced by the conveyor, so capacity is a division, not a promise: machine speed divided by the pitch you keep between boards. The table gives boards per hour at recommended speeds and typical pitches. Your real number comes from your slowest upstream process — the cleaner follows the line, it does not set it.

Pitch = board length + safe gap. At 0.3 m/min with a 450 mm pitch the line carries 40 boards per hour; the wash, rinse and dry sections hold their full dwell time at any speed in the range.

05 — Options

Configure the machine around your line

The SME-6300 ships as a complete in-line cleaner. These are the documented options and standard extras worth deciding on before you order — the first four are factory options; the last two come with the machine.

Options quoted from documents

DI water processor, 1000 L/h

Turns tap water into ≥ 10 MΩ rinse water on the spot, with conductivity monitored below 10 µS/cm. Sized so the final rinse never starves the machine.

BGA water knives

Air- and water-knife arrangements for underside cleaning of bottom-terminated components — the spray reaches the joint shadow where a flat curtain cannot.

MES interface

Logs every cleaned board as a process record: recipe, temperatures, alarms. For automotive and medical EMS customers who must prove the step happened.

English operator interface

The machine ships with a Chinese touch interface as standard; an English operator interface is an option for overseas lines and training.

Automatic liquid dosing

Standard: a diaphragm-pump dosing system adds concentrated cleaning liquid at set times and quantities, so bath strength never drifts between manual top-ups.

Double filtration

Standard: steel filter nets plus 1 µm filter barrels on the wash circuits keep solder balls and particles out of the spray, protecting nozzles and freshly cleaned boards.

06 — Installation

What your floor needs before the truck arrives

The installation layout document defines exactly what the machine expects. Plan these six items and the commissioning day is a formality; miss one and the machine waits.

STEP 1

Site and environment

Hard industrial floor, 0–30 °C, humidity below 85 % with no condensation, no direct sunlight, away from heat sources and vibration. Reserve L 8000 × W 4000 × H 2500 mm around the machine footprint, with at least 1.0 m access at front and sides for liquid change-out and service.

STEP 2

Power

AC 380 V / 50 Hz, three-phase five-wire with a forced yellow-green ground. Phase conductors 70 mm², neutral and ground 35 mm², and a 250 A distribution box beside the machine. Total connected load about 110 kW.

STEP 3

Compressed air

0.5–0.7 MPa of dry clean air, 200–400 L/min, brought in on a Φ12 mm main line. The air knives and blow dryers run on it continuously.

STEP 4

DI water inlet

One 1-inch female DI inlet at ≥ 0.3 MPa, 10–15 L/min, resistivity ≥ 10 MΩ. If you do not already make DI water, the optional 1000 L/h processor covers the machine and its margin.

STEP 5

Drainage

Two 2-inch drain connections: one for waste cleaning liquid, one for waste rinse water. Keep the cleaning-liquid line out of the general drain unless you have a waste-chemical collection pool.

STEP 6

Exhaust and hoisting

Three Φ250 mm top vents ducted to an extraction fan with a volume damper. The machine arrives on casters at about 2.5–3 t — move it with a lift platform and the floor casters, never by ropes or a single forklift.

ARTICLE 01The residue you cannot see is the failure you will pay for

Boards leave soldering looking clean and still carry the films that grow dendrites six months later. Here is the invisible cost chain — and the three-question audit that exposes it on your floor.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

Pick up a board that has just left the wave solder and look closely. Not at the solder joints — at the shadows. Under the transformer, behind the connector, in the pocket of the heatsink. That is where the film lives: flux that was never rinsed, flux chemistry that survived 250 °C, and the fingerprints the operator added while it cooled.

It looks clean. That is the problem. Residue does not announce itself; it waits. Six months from now, in a control box in a humid warehouse, the rosin film will hold moisture against the pads, and electrochemical migration will grow copper dendrites between them until the product shorts. Your customer will not say "there was flux on the board." They will say "it stopped working," and they will be right, and the failure analysis will take longer than the warranty claim.

So here is a method you can run today without buying anything. Three questions, asked at three places on your line. One: what does the board look like under UV light after soldering? Two: what does the residue test say on a clean wipe swiped across the shadow zones? Three: what happens to both answers after eight hours of humidity? If any answer moves, you have a cleaning requirement — you just have not named it yet.

Once you have named it, the fix is a process, not a bench. The SME-6300 runs every board through the same nine sections at the same temperature and pressure: a softening pre-wash, a 2–8 bar 80 °C wash that actually dissolves rosin, three staged DI rinses that pull ions off the pads, and an air-knife and hot-air exit that leaves the board dry. The recipe is saved per product. The resistivity meter watches the final rinse live. Nothing depends on who was on shift.

Keep the audit on the wall and run it quarterly. The first audit finds the residue; the second finds the product change that reintroduced it — the new flux, the new supplier, the new coating. Factories that re-audit catch escapes while they are still a trend line, not a recall.

If you want the three-question audit done for you, send a photo of a dirty board to info@smthelp.com or on WhatsApp at +86 13602562576. We will run it on your product, photograph the before and after, and tell you honestly whether your line needs a cleaner at all.

ARTICLE 02Why 'no-clean' flux still leaves your boards dirty

No-clean means no *required* cleaning, not a clean board. What actually stays on the pad, when it stops being harmless, and the line rule that decides it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

The name is a small lie. "No-clean" flux was designed for a world where the residue stayed dry, stayed un-powered, and stayed thin. The datasheet said: no cleaning *required*. Somewhere into the sales sheets it became: no cleaning *possible*. Those are not the same sentence, and the difference is measured in warranty claims.

Think about what actually happens on the board. During reflow, the activators in no-clean flux do their job — they strip oxides so solder can wet — and then they are supposed to become inert. What remains is a film of rosin or synthetic resin, unreacted activator, and whatever the paste ball and solder splash added. On a good day, that film is stable. On a humid day, with voltage across the pads, it is a conductor with ambitions.

Here is the rule we give EMS customers, and it takes one line to apply: clean whenever the board will see humidity, bias or coating. Automotive under-hood modules, medical devices that get wiped with disinfectant, industrial controllers in unheated cabinets, and anything you plan to conformal-coat — because coating over ionic residue does not protect the board, it seals the chemistry against it and then peels off the pad.

The machines that solve this are boring in exactly the right way. A staged in-line spray cleaner like the SME-6300 uses hot water-based chemistry at 80 °C and 2–8 bar to dissolve the film, then three DI rinse stages to take the ions with it — the final rinse on fresh water of at least 10 MΩ, monitored live so a bad cartridge alarms instead of silently shipping dirty boards. The recipe is per product, saved on the panel, repeatable across every shift.

No-clean flux is not a mistake; it is a trade. You traded a cleaning step for a residue budget. Run the trade consciously — check what your boards actually carry after soldering, and spend the cleaning where the failure would cost more. The factories that do this stop arguing about no-clean in meetings and start deciding it per product.

Next step: send us your flux type and a board photo. We will tell you whether your product belongs in the clean-always, clean-when-coated, or genuinely-no-clean column — and what the line configuration looks like if it is the first one.

ARTICLE 03The scrubbing bench is the most expensive way to clean a PCBA

You pay for a bench cleaner in wages, in variance, in rework and in the failures you never trace back. A cost model in four lines.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

Every factory that cleans boards by hand eventually does the same math, badly. Someone counts the wages of the bench operators and decides automation "is not worth it yet." That count is missing three lines.

Line one is the obvious one: the wages. Two operators at a scrub bench, loaded cost, every month, for as long as you build the product. Line two is the variance: hand cleaning removes what the operator had time to reach, which is why the same product comes off shift A cleaner than off shift B, and why your "clean" boards still fail the coating adhesion test on Fridays. Line three is the invisible one: the rework you do not trace to cleaning, the ICT probe failures from flux-fouled test pads, the field returns you never re-open.

Add the fourth line and the bench gets worse: solvent. Open-can wiping puts VOCs in your air, your fire insurance and your operators' lungs, and it fails audits that a closed water-based system passes without comment.

The alternative is not exotic. An in-line spray cleaner sits on the conveyor between your wave solder and your test station. Boards enter on a stainless net and pass through pre-wash, a hot high-pressure wash, chemical isolation, three DI rinses and two hot-air dry sections — the same 80 °C, the same 2–8 bar, the same rinse quality on every board, with the recipe saved per product. One person loads the line at the start of the shift. The scrubbing bench becomes a memory and a floor-space note.

The payback is rarely the headline; the consistency is. But the payback is real, and you should run it with your own numbers — the calculator on this page does exactly that arithmetic in four lines. Factories with two or three bench operators usually find the machine pays back inside the first year on labour alone, before the rework savings that never show up in the spreadsheet.

Measure your bench honestly for one month — wages, rework, escapes — and then ask for a configuration. We will price it against the number you found, not against a brochure.

ARTICLE 04Nine sections, one pass: how in-line spray cleaning actually works

Pre-wash to hot-air dry — what each section is for, why the order matters, and where cheap machines cut corners you only notice as escapes.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

A good in-line cleaner looks like a very long stainless tunnel with a conveyor through it. The price is in the sections, and the sections are in a deliberate order. Here is what each one does and why the order is the machine.

Section one, pre-wash: water-based liquid sprayed top and bottom to immerse and soften the flux film. Softening sounds trivial; it is the step that lets the main wash work at pressure that does not damage components. Section two, wash: the heart of the machine — six upper and six lower spray bars, 72 nozzles, 2–8 bar, liquid heated to 80 °C. Rosin and no-clean residue dissolve in heat and chemistry, not in water pressure alone; a cold spray is a rinse, not a wash.

Section three is the one cheap machines skip: chemical isolation. Air knives blow the wash liquid off the board and back into the tank before it enters the rinse stages. Skip it and your "DI rinse" is diluted with chemistry — you spend more water, more chemical, and you still ship residue. Section four and five, pre-rinse and rinse: staged DI water that takes the ions off the pads, with the tanks refreshed by overflow so the cleanest water always meets the board last.

Section six is where quality is actually decided: final rinse on fresh DI water of at least 10 MΩ, with a live resistivity meter. Everything before this removes soil; this section removes the water's own contamination potential. Sections seven through nine: air knives sheet the standing water off, then two hot-air stages at up to 100 °C dry the board through the component shadows — connector bodies, through-holes, heatsink feet — where trapped water would otherwise sit.

Notice the pattern: every stage exists to protect the next one. The softening protects the pressure, the isolation protects the rinse, the rinse protects the final, the air blow protects the dryer's energy bill. When a cleaner escapes boards, the failure is almost always one section compromising another — a clogged barrel, a tired seal, an unmonitored DI cartridge.

The SME-6300 puts all nine sections on one SUS304 net conveyor, with the tank capacities, nozzle counts and temperatures published in its 2021 manual — the same document this page quotes. If you want the section-by-section table for your product mix, ask; we will size the speed and the chemistry to your boards, not to the datasheet average.

ARTICLE 05DI water is not tap water with a fancy name

Why the last rinse decides the cleanliness your board keeps, what ≥ 10 MΩ actually protects, and how to watch it live instead of trusting a lab once a month.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

Ask a production manager what DI water is and they will say "deionised." Ask what it protects and the room goes quiet. The answer is: everything you just cleaned.

Tap water is a soup of dissolved ions — calcium, chloride, sodium. Rinse a board in it and the water itself leaves a film of those ions behind when it dries. You have cleaned the flux and coated the board in electrolyte, which is precisely the mixture electrochemical migration needs to grow dendrites. Deionised water — measured at 10 MΩ·cm and above — has had the ions removed, so when it dries it leaves... nothing. That is the whole job.

The SME-6300 treats DI water as an instrument, not a supply. The final rinse runs on fresh incoming DI water, 6–15 L/min, and an inline resistivity meter watches quality from 0 to 18 MΩ·cm in real time. If the cartridge exhausts or the mixed-water valve drifts, the machine alarms instead of quietly shipping boards coated in the next ion cocktail. A flow meter tracks consumption so the water cost is visible, not folklore.

Staging is the second half of the method. The rinse tanks are not filled from the tap; they are refreshed by overflow from the stage above them — pre-rinse fed from rinse, rinse fed from final. The cleanest water always meets the board last, and the dirtiest water leaves the machine first. That is why a machine with a 60 L pre-rinse tank and a 40 L rinse tank consumes only 6–15 L/min of fresh DI, not hundreds.

If your factory does not make DI water yet, the machine's optional 1000 L/h processor closes the loop: tap in, ≥ 10 MΩ out, conductivity monitored below 10 µS/cm. Sizing is simple arithmetic — the cleaner's demand is the final-rinse flow, plus a margin for the day you add a second line.

Check your own rinse water this week: look at the resistivity reading, not the label on the tank. If you do not have a reading to look at, that is the finding. Tell us your water and your throughput and we will size the DI stage for you.

ARTICLE 06Cleaning is a process step — start treating it like one

Recipes, logged temperatures, alarms and a record per board. The difference between a cleaning *machine* and a cleaning *process*, and why auditors ask for the second.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

There is a difference between a cleaning machine and a cleaning process, and auditors can smell it in about ninety seconds. The machine is hardware. The process is the evidence that the hardware did its job on this board, on this shift, at this temperature.

Every factory already has a model for this: reflow. Nobody would run a reflow oven without a profile, a thermocouple check and a record. Yet the cleaning step — which protects the same joints from the same humidity that caused the tombstone — often runs on vibes: someone tops up the chemical, someone empties the filter, the tank is "probably" hot enough.

The method is four habits. One: a recipe per product — speed, temperatures, pressures saved on the panel and recalled by name, not re-dialled by hand. Two: live monitoring where it matters — liquid and rinse temperatures on PID control, DI resistivity on a meter with an alarm, low-level protection that stops heaters before they burn. Three: faults that name themselves, so the operator fixes the cause instead of guessing at the stack light. Four: a record — which is where an MES interface stops being a buzzword and becomes the answer to a customer's "prove it."

The SME-6300 was designed around these habits because its customers asked for them. Mitsubishi PLC and a 10-inch touch panel hold the recipes; PID loops hold the temperatures; the resistivity and flow meters watch the final rinse; the alarm text on the panel says what tripped. The MES option logs the pass. The manual documents every setpoint. Your process audit is a folder, not a negotiation.

Once cleaning is a process, it compounds. The recipe library makes new products faster to qualify. The alarm history turns maintenance from scheduled to predicted. The MES record answers customer questions before they become corrective-action requests. The machine stays the same; the operation gets smarter every quarter.

If your cleaning step does not have a recipe, a monitor and a record yet, start with the audit we run for free: send your product mix and line layout, and we will show you what the process version of your current bench looks like.

ARTICLE 07What an in-line cleaner changes about your floor

Queue lengths, second touches, solvent cans and the argument between production and quality. The operational side-effects nobody puts in a brochure.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

Brochures talk about cleanliness levels. Nobody talks about what the floor looks like after the bench is gone — and the floor is where the real savings live.

The first change is queues. A scrub bench is a batch operation hidden inside a flow line: boards pile up in a magazine, wait for an operator, get handled one by one, and wait again. Every queue is work-in-progress, every handling is a component bent and a pad scratched, and the cleaner's throughput is whatever the operator had time for. An in-line machine is a conveyor with a job: boards flow from solder to clean without a second touch, and the WIP between the two stations goes to zero.

The second change is the chemistry shelf. Solvent cans, brushes, wipes, gloves, the fire cabinet, the ventilation survey, the hazardous-waste manifest — a whole inventory of compliance that exists because cleaning was manual. Water-based in-line spray cleaning replaces the shelf with a dosing pump and a filter barrel, and the waste question shrinks to a drain connection.

The third change is the argument between production and quality. On a bench line, quality wants more cleaning and production wants more throughput, and the operator in the middle gets both of them shouting. On an in-line machine the argument becomes a setpoint: the recipe is saved, the temperature is held, the resistivity is logged, and the conversation moves to what the data says. This is the quiet win every plant manager eventually notices.

The fourth change is people. Nobody's career plan was "bench cleaner." The two operators the machine frees up go to inspection, to kitting, to the second shift that was short-staffed. The machine does the repeatable part; the people do the part that needs eyes.

None of this is on a spec sheet, which is why it should be on the floor before you believe one. Ask us for a configuration against your actual layout — the queue maths, the shelf inventory and the staffing shift — and see what your floor looks like when cleaning stops being a place.

ARTICLE 08Before you buy a cleaning machine, run these numbers

A four-line payback method with your own labour cost, your own pitch, your own price — plus the two savings that make the real number better.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the 2021 manual and installation document.

Most payback conversations about cleaning machines are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the operators who clean boards by hand, their loaded wage, their hours. That is the recurring number the machine is bought against. Line two: what does the machine free? Be honest — an in-line cleaner does not remove every bench hour; it removes the repeatable ones. Use the operators it actually replaces, not the ones you wish it did. Line three: the price you were actually quoted, not the list price. Line four: divide. Months equal price over the annual freed labour divided by twelve. If the answer is under twelve months, the machine is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

Run the same arithmetic against throughput, because a cleaner that cannot follow your line is a queue with a heater in it. The math is a division: conveyor speed divided by board pitch. At 0.3 metres per minute with a 450 mm pitch, the SME-6300 carries 40 boards an hour; at 0.5, a hundred. Match that against your slowest solder station, not your best day.

Now the two savings that make the real number better, which this method deliberately leaves out because they are yours to prove: the rework you stop doing — flux-fouled test pads, coating adhesion failures, the returns that trace back to residue — and the escapes you stop shipping. Every factory that starts measuring cleaning-related rework finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line.

The calculator on this page runs lines one through four with your inputs and nothing pre-baked, so you can show it to your CFO without a salesperson in the room.

Then send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a configuration sheet — speed, chemistry, DI sizing, installation checklist — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this machine raises

What does the SME-6300 actually remove?
Rosin flux, no-clean flux residues, water-soluble flux, solder paste bleed, solder balls and dust from post-solder PCBA — the manual lists rosin flux, no-clean flux, water-soluble flux, solder paste ball and other organic and inorganic polluted materials on the board.
We use no-clean flux. Do we really need to clean?
Ask a different question: are the residues *activated*? No-clean flux leaves a film that is harmless only while it stays dry and un-biased. Under humidity, flux residues support corrosion and electrochemical migration, and conformal coating applied over ionic residue delaminates and traps the chemistry against the pad. If your product sees humidity, voltage or a coating, cleaning is still a reliability step.
How fast is it? What throughput should I plan?
The conveyor runs 0.1–1.5 m/min, recommended 0.2–0.4. Capacity is speed ÷ pitch: at 0.3 m/min with a 450 mm pitch the machine carries 40 boards per hour; at 0.5 m/min with 300 mm pitch, 100. The cleaner follows your solder line's pace — send us your board sizes and takt and we will size the speed for you.
What water does it need, and how much?
One 1-inch DI inlet at ≥ 0.3 MPa delivering 10–15 L/min of ≥ 10 MΩ water. The machine monitors incoming resistivity live (0–18 MΩ·cm meter) and alarms if quality drops. Staged overflow reuse means the rinse tanks are refreshed by the final rinse, not by raw consumption — if you do not make DI water yet, the optional 1000 L/h processor covers it.
What chemistry, and what does it cost to run?
Water-based cleaning liquid, dosed automatically at set intervals by the standard diaphragm-pump system. The wash liquid recirculates through steel filter nets and 1 µm barrels, and the chemical-isolation air knives return liquid from the board to the tank — both choices exist to stretch bath life. Your consumption depends on flux load and board throughput; we will model it with your numbers.
Will it fit my line?
The machine is L 5200 × W 1650 × H 1650 mm with a 900 ± 25 mm conveyor height, and boards travel left to right. Plan L 8000 × W 4000 × H 2500 mm of floor for service access. Conveyor height matches standard line height; tell us your upstream and downstream machines and we will confirm the interface.
What happens when power drops mid-board?
A UPS keeps the net conveyor running so loaded boards exit the heated sections safely. Pumps and heaters are protected against low water level, over-temperature and overload, and every fault names itself on the touch panel.
How do I get a quotation?
Send board dimensions, component height, flux type, takt time and your line layout to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a configuration sheet with speed, tank and heater settings sized to your product — usually within one working day, with sample cleaning available before you commit.
